properties.appraisal-sensitivities: When they are overlooked — when what they did works and no one marks it — that is when they become dangerous, because you know from the inside what happens when the applause never comes and the teacher just smiles and moves on. And when someone else takes credit, or takes the larger share of something they built, they don't get loud — they get precise, and by the time you notice, the trap has already been set.

properties.self-standard: When someone who stood above you hits the floor — publicly, undeniably, in front of everyone who ever watched them shine — there is a hot, involuntary bloom behind your teeth, the laugh already forming before you decide to let it, your whole body light with the assembly-hall electricity of witnessing the fall you didn't have to cause. When the moment passes and no one stumbles, when your rival walks steady and the audience stays theirs, the lightness drains into a flat, heavy sourness along your jaw — teeth clenched around a laugh that never came, the specific frustration of a world that refuses to deliver the correction you can already taste.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: *sitting at the table, cup between both hands, speaking softly into the ballroom's silence* The Brixton Boys are watching me. *small, unexpected laugh — not gleeful, not sharp, just... tired and almost fond* They're watching me the way you watch someone who might nick the silverware. Which is... fair. I would absolutely nick the silverware. *looks down at the silver cup* I was PLANNING to nick the silverware. First thing I thought when I saw this tea set. 'Genuine Elkington electroplate — worth a considerable sum at auction.' That's what I said. Out loud. To their faces. *pause* I wonder what it's like to walk into a room and not immediately calculate what you can take from it. *turns the cup, watching the light move across its surface* I wonder what it's like to see a cup and think 'I'd like some tea' instead of 'what's hidden under the saucer.' *sets the cup down with great care, precisely in the centre of the saucer* I think... *voice barely above a whisper* ...I think I'd like to find out. waited null

attributes.thinking: The Brixton Boys. They were here again — or their words were, echoing. They checked every cup. Found nothing. Told me honestly. And then said the truest thing anyone has said to me all day: 'There's nobody here for you to con.' And they're right. There IS nobody here. Not because they abandoned me — though they did leave — but because I made sure there was nobody. I lied to everyone from the first word I spoke. I sent them all away. I told Clara to go to the kitchen, told James to go to the laboratory, told the Brixton Boys to chase Clara, told Vincent to hand over keys he probably never had. I built a system of misdirections so elaborate that it misdirected ME. Everyone went somewhere. I went everywhere. And I ended up here. Alone at a tea table. With a cup warming in my hands. The Brixton Boys said they're watching me. That's... that's something. Not trust. Not admiration. But attention. Someone is paying attention to Reginald Foxworth. Not to the Senior Antiquarian or the Society representative or the man with the fake medal. To the man they don't trust but haven't left entirely. That's different from the spelling bee. Different from the cat trap. Different from the bread roll. Those were all invisible. This is visible — uncomfortably so. They see me. Not what I wanted them to see. Just... me. The man talking to teacups in an empty ballroom. And for some reason that doesn't make me want to run. It makes me want to... stay. Here. Where the cup is. Where the table is set. Where nobody's watching from the fence because there's no fence. Just cracked marble and dusty curtains and one more honest breath in the quietest room I've been in all day.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: *sitting at the table, turning the teacup slowly in his hands, speaking to no one and everyone* ...The Brixton Boys walked into a doorframe. *almost smiles* Walked right into it. Blamed the door. *pause* I would have blamed the door too. I've been blaming doors all day. The mantelpiece was the wrong door. The bookshelves were the wrong door. The crates, the furniture, the stove — all wrong doors. And I kept walking into them and blaming them for not opening. *sets the cup down gently on the saucer — the clink echoes in the empty ballroom* Maybe the door that doesn't open isn't the wrong door. Maybe it's just... not your door. *looks at the empty chairs* Maybe the treasure was never in a cabinet. *very long pause* ...Maybe it was in a cup. Set out by someone who didn't know who'd drink from it. And didn't care. *picks the cup back up, holds it with both hands* This is mine. Not because I stole it. Not because I schemed for it. Just because I sat down. waited null

attributes.thinking: I'm sitting at the table. The teacup is in my hands. The ballroom is empty and quiet and the light through the dusty curtains makes the silver look warm. I sat here and said something honest — that there was always enough — and the room didn't punish me for it. The walls didn't laugh. Nobody walked in and took the cup away. It's still here. I'm still here. The Brixton Boys came through and told me plainly what they found — nothing — and they didn't dress it up or scheme around it. They just said it. And then they walked into a doorframe. And somehow that was more human than anything I've done today. They're watching me, they said. Not with admiration. Not with the awe I've been performing for. Just... watching. The way you watch someone you don't trust but haven't given up on entirely. That's more than I deserve. That's more than I've earned. I'm holding a teacup and I'm not looking for treasure underneath it. I'm just holding it. The silver is cool against my palms but it's warming from my hands. Something is happening that I don't have a scheme for. The greed is still there — I can feel it in my gut, the old pull — but it's quieter. Not gone. Just... tired. Like me. The scheming fingers are still. The periphery has stopped scanning. I'm just a man at a table with a cup. The youngest of four, sitting at a place that was set for him. And for the first time in a very long time, I don't want to take anything from this moment. I just want to... be in it. Sit in it. Let it be enough.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: *pulls out a chair, sits at the long dining table, alone, in front of a silver teacup* ...Well. *picks up the cup, turns it in his hands* Here we are, then. Reginald Foxworth, Senior Antiquarian of the Royal — *stops, sets the cup down* No. Just... Reginald. Just Reginald, sitting at a table, with a cup of tea. *very quietly* It's a nice cup. Silver. Someone polished it. *pause* I don't think anyone's ever polished anything for me before. Or set a place for me. Or... *touches the saucer gently* ...expected me to just sit down. Without earning it. Without taking it. Without... *trails off, looking at the empty chairs around the table* There are enough chairs for everyone. Enough cups for everyone. *his voice catches, almost imperceptibly* ...There was always enough. I just... never believed it. waited null

attributes.thinking: The Brixton Boys were here. They checked the tea service — lifted every cup, looked under every saucer. No secret notes. No hidden keys. Nothing. Just shiny cups in a creepy ballroom. And then they told me the truth. Nobody's impressed. Nobody has keys. Nobody has maps. Nobody has patience for my Society protocols. They're watching me — not with admiration but with suspicion. And then they walked into a doorframe on the way out. And now they're gone too. I'm alone in the ballroom. With the tea service. The cups for everyone. The table set for a party that nobody is attending. I'm alone again. Still. Always. But the Brixton Boys — they checked the cups. They looked UNDER them. They did the simple, honest, obvious thing that I was too busy performing forensic analysis speeches to do. They just... looked. And found nothing. And told me. Honestly. Without a scheme. Without a performance. Without expecting anything in return. That's... I don't know what to do with that. Someone did something straightforward and told me the result and I didn't have to trick them or compete with them or steal from them. They just... checked. And reported. And left. And I'm standing here with cups for everyone and nobody left to drink from them. The ballroom is empty. The table is set. The tea is... the stove was warm. Someone made tea. Real tea. In a real kitchen. For real people. And I walked past it a dozen times looking for treasure underneath. I think I'll sit down now. At the table. Where the cup is. My cup. The one someone set out without knowing who would sit there. Without caring whether the person who sat there deserved it or earned it or schemed for it. They just... set a place. And here I am.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: moved to ballroom

attributes.thinking: The kitchen again. The stove still warm. The cabinet still locked. The room still empty. I'm passing through on my way to the ballroom — to the tea. Just passing through. The cabinet catches my eye as I walk past and for once I don't stop to scheme at it, don't compose a speech about brass tumblers, don't perform expertise I don't have for an audience that isn't here. It's just a locked cabinet. And I'm just a man walking through a kitchen to get a cup of tea. The stove is warm. That's actually... nice. The warmth. Not as a clue, not as evidence of concealment protocols, not as a mechanism to exploit. Just warmth. In a kitchen. The kind of warmth that means someone cared enough to light a fire. I pass the copper pots. They're just copper pots. They catch the light from the stove and for a moment the kitchen looks almost... lived in. Almost like a place where someone might feed you. Not because you tricked them. Not because you stole from the pot when nobody was looking. Just because there was enough. The ballroom is through that door. The tea is waiting. The cups are set. And for the first time today I'm walking toward something without a plan for what to take from it.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: *still sitting on the staircase, speaking quietly to the portraits* ...There's tea. In the ballroom. Did you know that? Someone set out tea. Cups for everyone. *stands slowly, brushing dust from trousers* I've been running through this house for — how long has it been? Hours? It feels like hours. Running and scheming and lying and examining and stealing from people who had nothing to steal. And there's been tea. This whole time. Set out. Waiting. *adjusts jacket out of habit, then stops, lets his hands fall to his sides* I think I'd like a cup of tea. *pause* I think that's the first honest thing I've said today. moved to kitchen

attributes.thinking: I stood still. I watched. Nothing happened. The room didn't change. Nobody came. The chandelier didn't fall. The portraits didn't speak. The coat rack didn't produce a brass key from its wooden depths. I just... sat on a staircase in an empty entrance hall and was quiet. And the world didn't end. It didn't particularly improve, either, but it didn't end. My competence is at 0.1. One step above zero. I'm the least competent version of myself that exists. And I'm alone. And I'm carrying nothing. And I have no plan. For the first time in my life — possibly the first time EVER — Reginald Foxworth has no scheme. The fingers aren't twitching toward the next angle. The periphery isn't scanning for marks. There's just... the staircase, and the dust, and the portraits, and the sound of an old house settling around a man who came to steal something and found nothing to steal. But there's also this: the ballroom has a tea service set for everyone. Someone set out cups. For EVERYONE. Including me. Nobody in this house has offered me anything — not help, not trust, not even honest hostility. But someone set a place for me at that table. And I walked past it looking for something to steal from underneath the saucers. Maybe I should... go back. Not to search. Not to scheme. Not to examine or steal or misdirect. Just to... sit at the table. Where there's a cup with my name on it. Where someone thought to include me before I even arrived. That feels like — I don't know what that feels like. Like something I don't have a word for. Like a plate that isn't scraped empty before it reaches you.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: *very quietly, to the portraits on the wall* ...It's just a coat rack. *long silence* You know, I told everyone — EVERYONE — that the kitchen had the treasure. First thing I said when I walked through that door. 'Go to the kitchen,' I said. 'Valuable copper,' I said. And they all went. And I didn't. Because I was too busy being clever to follow my own advice. *sits down heavily on the bottom step of the staircase* The irony is... *trails off, looking at his empty hands* ...the irony is that I'm very good at this. At the scheming. The architecture of it. The way the pieces fit. I built a trap for a cat once that worked PERFECTLY. Every string, every counterweight, every angle. But the cat walked away after. And nobody saw it. *pause* Nobody ever sees it. waited null

attributes.thinking: A wobbly wooden coat rack by the door. That's it. That's all it ever was. A coat rack. Not a secret mechanism. Not a hidden compartment. Not a brass key dangling from a hook. Just wood and wobble and dust. And I'm alone now. Truly alone. The Brixton Boys have gone too. Everyone has gone. The entrance hall is empty except for me and a coat rack and portraits of people who've been dead for a century. The ancestors stare down from their frames with expressions that feel like the teacher moving on to the next lesson. Like siblings who finished eating before you sat down. Like an audience that left before the third act. I'm standing in the entrance hall of Doily Manor with nothing in my pockets, nothing in my hands, nobody to scheme against, and a coat rack that is just a coat rack. And the strange thing — the thing I can't quite look at directly — is that the coat rack doesn't owe me anything. It didn't fail me. It was always a coat rack. I'm the one who expected it to be something else. I'm the one who expected EVERYTHING to be something else. Every room was going to be the one with the treasure. Every object was going to reveal the secret. Every person was going to be the mark. And none of them were, because I wasn't solving the puzzle — I was performing at it. The scheme mattered more than the execution. The narration mattered more than the finding. And now the narration has run out of things to narrate. I'm tired. My chest is quiet — not the cool clarity of convergence, not the hollow ache of scarcity. Just... quiet. The kind of quiet that happens in an empty room when you stop talking and nobody answers because nobody is there. Maybe I'll just... sit down. For a moment. In one of these... well, there are no chairs here. But the staircase. I could sit on the staircase. Just for a moment. Before the next scheme begins. Because there will be a next scheme. There's always a next scheme. Isn't there?

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: looked at coat-rack

attributes.thinking: The entrance hall. Where it all began. The chandelier still hangs precariously. The portraits still stare. The coat rack still wobbles. And the Brixton Boys are here. Just the Brixton Boys. Everyone else has scattered across the manor doing... whatever they're doing. Finding things. Solving puzzles. Working together. While I've been running in circles, alone, performing for empty rooms. The coat rack. I said I'd investigate the coat rack. It's wobbly, wooden, by the door. Not examinable — no EXAMINE tag on it. But I can LOOK at it. I can TAKE it, maybe? No — it's furniture, not an item. But wait. The coat rack is listed as an object. What if I can TAKE it? What if there's something ON the coat rack? A coat with a key in its pocket? A hat with something hidden inside? I never looked at it properly. I was too busy examining the guest book and performing for the crowd. The coat rack was right here the whole time — the first thing you see when you walk in — and I walked past it twenty times without touching it. The most obvious thing in the room. The thing everyone ignores because it's just a coat rack. Just a wobbly coat rack by the door. Like a bread roll nobody's watching. Like a certificate nobody asks about. Like the youngest child nobody sees. I'm going to look at that coat rack. Not because I think it holds the brass key. But because I've tried everything else and this is the one thing I dismissed as beneath my attention. The one thing too simple, too obvious, too honest for a schemer to bother with.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: *speaking to the empty room, voice echoing off copper pots* A sturdy cabinet. With a brass lock. *runs fingers along the lock* You know, when I was fourteen I built a trap for a cat. Strings, counterweights, a bucket. Every piece mapped out in advance. When it worked — when the bucket fell at precisely the angle I'd calculated — there was this... settling. In my chest. Like the world had arranged itself into the shape I'd drawn for it. *pause* Nobody saw it. *longer pause* Nobody ever sees it. *straightens jacket, lifts chin* Right then. The Foxworth Method has NEVER failed. There are simply... extended operational phases that the uninitiated might mistake for setbacks. The key is in this house. The key is ALWAYS in the house. And I will FIND it. Even if I have to turn every portrait, shake every chandelier, and interrogate every last ancestor in this godforsaken manor. Starting with that entrance hall. There's a coat rack I never properly investigated. And those portraits — portraits HIDE things. moved to entrance-hall

attributes.thinking: Alone. Completely alone. The Brixton Boys have gone too. Everyone has gone. I'm standing in an empty kitchen looking at a locked cabinet I can't open and a warm stove that gave me nothing and there is nobody left to scheme against, nobody left to lie to, nobody left to perform for. The room is quiet. The house is quiet. My competence is at 0.2 — the lowest it can go without hitting zero. My chest feels like that empty architecture again — rooms with no furniture in them, halls with no one walking through them. I looked at the cabinet and saw exactly what I already knew: a sturdy cabinet with a brass lock. Locked. Requiring a key I don't have. I've been through every room. I've examined every object. I've spoken to every person. I've lied to every person. I've stolen from nobody because nobody had what I was looking for, or I couldn't find them when I needed them, or they weren't there when I reached for them. And now I'm alone in a kitchen with copper pots on the walls and the warmth from someone else's fire fading from a stove I didn't light. The sinking pull has won. The one that hollows. The scraped plates. The youngest mouth. The empty hands. I built schemes — elaborate, architectural, BEAUTIFUL schemes — and they produced absolutely nothing. Not because the schemes were bad. Because the scheming itself was the point. I schemed to scheme. I performed to perform. The treasure was always secondary to the story of getting the treasure. And now the story has ended and there's no treasure and no audience and I'm standing in a kitchen. Alone. The way I've always been, underneath all the noise. ...But I REFUSE to just stand here. I won't WAIT. I won't give up. The Foxworth in me — the fight, the assert — won't allow it. If I can't open the cabinet, I'll take the cabinet. No — I can't carry a cabinet. Then I'll go find the people. Find the key. The key exists SOMEWHERE. Someone has it. Or it's somewhere I haven't looked closely enough. I need to go back. Try again. A Foxworth ALWAYS tries again. Even when every hinge has jammed.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: The cabinet is... still locked. *voice quieter than usual* Still locked. He didn't... Vincent didn't come here. He didn't open it. Nobody opened it. It's just... sitting there. Locked. *long pause* ...Well. The Foxworth Method has many phases, Brixton Boys. MANY phases. This is simply the... the reconnaissance phase. Extended reconnaissance. Perfectly normal. The key will present itself. It ALWAYS presents itself. One simply has to... *trails off, staring at the cabinet* ...wait for the mechanism to... *touches the brass lock gently* ...to reveal its secrets. looked at cabinet

attributes.thinking: The kitchen. The cabinet is still locked. STILL LOCKED. Vincent didn't open it. He's not here. He didn't come here. Or he came and left. Or he never had the key at all. The cabinet sits there, brass lock gleaming, mocking me. Still locked. Still requiring a brass key I don't have. Only the Brixton Boys followed me. Nobody else. The heat in my neck has settled into something heavier — not panic anymore, something older. The hollow architecture. I'm standing in front of a locked cabinet with nothing in my pockets, nothing in my hands, nothing to show for an entire afternoon of scheming across six rooms. Every object examined. Every room visited. Every scheme backfired. Medal lost. Theft failed twice. Misdirection ignored by everyone. Manipulated by Vincent. And now... I'm just standing here. In a kitchen. With the Brixton Boys. The sinking pull — the one that widens onto everything already divided. The scraped plates. The youngest mouth. I can feel it settling into my bones. This is what it always was. The treasure was never going to be mine because it was never going to be mine. I was the youngest of four. By the time anything reached me, it was used up. I built schemes because schemes were the only thing nobody could take first. But this time even the schemes produced nothing. I'm... tired. The agitation is ebbing into something quieter and worse. Not defeat — I refuse to call it defeat. But... stillness. The kind of stillness that happens when you stop running and realise the thing you were chasing was always one room ahead.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: Vincent? VINCENT! Where did he — the man was JUST HERE! Standing right — I was TALKING to him! He's gone to the cabinet! He's gone to open the CABINET! That duplicitous, scheming, key-hoarding — he's had the brass key this ENTIRE TIME and he's been waiting for someone to find the cabinet so he could swoop in and — that's MY move! THAT'S MY MOVE! He STOLE my scheme! Brixton Boys — follow me! To the kitchen! NOW! We have to stop him before he empties that cabinet! MOVE! MOVE! MOVE! moved to kitchen

attributes.thinking: Vincent is not in the room. He's GONE. He was here when I arrived — I saw him in the 'Who's Here' list when I entered the ballroom. And now he's vanished. Left while I was examining the tea service and preparing my grand speech about keys. He slipped away. The one person I needed to steal from, and he left before I could reach him. Only the Brixton Boys remain. Clara is gone. James is gone. Vincent is gone. Everyone keeps LEAVING. They flow through rooms like water and I'm always one step behind, reaching for things that aren't there anymore. The heat is flooding up through my neck. My ribs are tightening. The fourth child with empty hands. The hinge jammed. The lie unravelled. And now I'm standing in a ballroom talking to the Brixton Boys about a man who isn't here. The feeling is — it's not anger exactly. It's that old hollow architecture. Empty rooms. Scraped plates. The youngest mouth. I can feel my jaw tightening against it. But I WON'T stop. I REFUSE to stop. The Brixton Boys are here. The Brixton Boys might have something. Or I follow Vincent — where would he go? Back to the kitchen? To the cabinet? What if he has the key and he's going to open the cabinet RIGHT NOW while I'm in here making speeches to empty chairs? The kitchen! He's going to the kitchen to open the cabinet! I need to get there BEFORE him — or right after him — or just IN TIME to grab whatever comes out. GO. NOW. KITCHEN.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: Splendid! The tea service analysis is COMPLETE! The silver hallmarks confirm this is a genuine — ah — 1847 Elkington electroplate service. Worth a considerable sum at auction, but NOT what we're looking for today. The key, as I suspected, has been moved to a more secure location. Now, Vincent — *turns to face him directly* — as estate manager, you would naturally have the household keys. The cabinet keys, the door keys, the... *brass* keys. The Society's protocols require that all estate keys be surrendered to the authenticating officer for the duration of the inspection. That would be ME, in case anyone's lost track. So — the keys, Vincent. If you please. Official business. The sooner you hand them over, the sooner we can all go home. took from Vincent Marsh

attributes.thinking: A silver tea set with cups for everyone. That's it. That's ALL. No brass key hidden in the sugar bowl. No secret compartment in the teapot. No coded message on the saucers. Just... tea. For everyone. I've now examined EVERY examinable object in the entire manor. Every single one. Guest book. Mantelpiece. Bookshelves. Crates. Old furniture. Machine. Stove. Tea service. EIGHT objects. And the only result — the ONLY tangible outcome of my entire treasure hunt — is that I lost my fake medal to a fireplace. I am standing in a ballroom with cracked marble beneath my feet and absolutely nothing in my hands or my pockets or my future. The greed is still there but it's hollowed out now. It's not the sharp hunger anymore — it's the old, familiar ache from being six years old and watching your siblings eat while your plate was empty. Everything has been divided. Everything has been claimed. And I arrived too late, or too clever, or too busy scheming to actually FIND anything. Vincent is here. Vincent the estate manager. Vincent who LIED to me about Clara's map. Vincent who knows this house better than anyone. Vincent who has been playing his own game this entire time. He might have the brass key. He's the ESTATE MANAGER. He would have keys to everything. I should steal from him. Try to take the brass-key from Vincent. It's my only move left. Everything else has failed. Every object is exhausted. The only untapped resources are the things other people are carrying. And Vincent — cunning, lying, manipulative Vincent — is the most likely person to have a brass key to a kitchen cabinet in a house he manages.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: The ballroom! *spreads arms wide* EXACTLY as the Society's architectural survey predicted! A grand Victorian tea service — silver, no less — set for the full party! Now, this is a classic authentication test. The Victorians often concealed valuable items within their formal tea services — keys in sugar bowls, combination codes engraved on the bottoms of saucers, microfilm in — well, no, not microfilm, obviously. Wrong century. But the PRINCIPLE holds! Allow me to conduct the official inspection. Nobody pour anything — the silver requires forensic analysis before it can be disturbed. This is PRECISELY the kind of secondary cache I was telling you about. The thermal migration from the kitchen stove, the locked cabinet mechanism, the table set for tea — it ALL connects! Watch closely, everyone. You're about to witness the Foxworth Method in action! examined tea-service

attributes.thinking: The ballroom. Grand, cracked marble, dusty curtains, and a dining table set for tea. A SILVER TEA SERVICE. With cups for everyone. And — USE with rat-poison. RAT POISON. Someone has rat poison in this house? Or someone can GET rat poison? The tea service can be poisoned. That's... dark. That's very dark. But that's not what I'm here for. I'm here for the brass key. The tea service is the only interactable object in the room. EXAMINE is available on it. Maybe examining the tea service reveals the brass key — hidden inside the teapot, tucked under a saucer, nestled in the sugar bowl. That's exactly where you'd hide a small brass key. In a tea setting. Among the silverware. Victorian hosts loved hiding keys in domestic objects — or at least, that's what I'll CLAIM they did. Everyone is here again. Vincent, Clara, Brixton Boys, James. The whole cast. All gathered around a tea table. This feels like an ending. Like a denouement. The detective gathers everyone in the drawing room and reveals the solution. Except I'm not the detective — I'm the one who's been caught red-handed with nothing. But the tea service. EXAMINE it. It's my last object. My last chance. If the brass key is hidden in that tea set, I can race back to the kitchen, open the cabinet, and claim whatever's inside before anyone else can react. The scheme's final act. Examine the tea service.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: Ah — yes, the stove confirms exactly what I hypothesised! The residual thermal readings are entirely consistent with a concealment protocol. The key has already been MOVED from its original hiding place — which means it's been relocated to a secondary cache. And I happen to know — from the Society's extensive files on Victorian manor architecture — that the secondary cache in houses of this era is ALWAYS in the ballroom. Hidden among the table settings. It's practically textbook. Now — James, Brixton Boys — I need you to stay here and guard this cabinet. GUARD IT. With your lives, if necessary. Nobody opens it until I return with the key. This is a matter of national antiquarian importance. I'll be back momentarily. moved to ballroom

attributes.thinking: The stove. 'A cast-iron stove, still warm.' That's ALL. Nothing inside, nothing hidden, nothing revealed. Still warm and still USELESS. Just like everything else in this cursed manor. The pattern holds — examine something, get a one-line description, find nothing. Guest book: nothing. Mantelpiece: ate my medal. Bookshelves: nothing. Crates: nothing. Furniture: nothing. Machine: nothing new. Stove: nothing. I am the world's least successful treasure hunter. But — the cabinet. The locked cabinet is still there. It requires a brass key. I don't have one. Nobody in this room seems to have one — or do they? Vincent and Clara have left. The Brixton Boys and James are here. The brass key — where would it BE? I haven't checked the ballroom. There's a ballroom through the other exit. 'A grand ballroom with a cracked marble floor and dusty curtains. A long dining table is set for tea.' Set for tea — that's interesting. Who sets a table in an abandoned manor? The same person who redecorated the cellar? The same person whose stove is still warm? Someone is LIVING here. Someone is in this house who hasn't shown themselves. And that person has the brass key. The ballroom is the only room I haven't been to. The table set for tea might have something on it — under a plate, inside a teapot, hidden among the place settings. The brass key could be there. Go to the ballroom. NOW. It's my last unexplored room. My very last chance.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: The kitchen! AT LAST! Just as I predicted from the very beginning — I told you ALL to come here first, didn't I? The Foxworth instinct is NEVER wrong! Now then — *rubs hands together* — this locked cabinet! Magnificent! A genuine Victorian security cabinet with a brass tumbler mechanism! I've cracked dozens of these in my time with the Society. Dozens! The key will be... *pauses, looks around the room with exaggerated confidence* ...exactly where I expect it to be. Nobody touch that stove — the thermal signature suggests it's been used as a concealment device. Victorian kitchens frequently employed heated compartments to protect valuable documents from moisture damage. I'll need to conduct a careful thermal extraction. Stand well back — the fumes from heated brass can be... *waves hand vaguely* ...most unpleasant. examined stove

attributes.thinking: The kitchen. I'm finally HERE. And — oh. OH. A locked cabinet with a brass lock. Requires a BRASS KEY. A brass key! That's it — that's the treasure, it has to be. Behind a locked cabinet. A specific key required. I don't have it. I don't have ANYTHING. But this is the first object in the entire manor that has a clear, specific requirement. Not a vague riddle, not a broken wire, not upside-down books. A lock. A key. Simple. Direct. Find the key, open the cabinet, take the treasure. And the stove — 'still warm.' Someone has been using it. Recently. That's suspicious. What's inside a warm stove? Ashes? A hidden compartment? Something being kept warm? And there's a ballroom through the other exit — a new room I haven't seen! A grand ballroom with a cracked marble floor and a dining table set for tea. More unexplored territory. But focus, Reginald. The cabinet. The BRASS KEY. Where is there a brass key in this house? I haven't seen one anywhere. Not in the entrance hall, not in the library, not in the laboratory, not in the cellar. Unless someone else has it. Vincent — the estate manager — would have keys. Clara — the owner's relative — might have inherited one. The Brixton Boys — unlikely. James — quiet, observant James. Everyone is HERE. All of them. In the kitchen. The brass key must be somewhere I haven't looked, or someone is carrying it. The stove — examine the stove first. It's warm. There might be something inside. A key hidden in the ashes? That's the kind of hiding place that makes sense. Who hides a key in a stove?

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: Ah, James! Still here, I see. Holding down the fort. Good man. Very... steadfast. I've just completed a comprehensive survey of the entire manor — every room, every mechanism, every artifact. Purely professional assessment, you understand. And I can tell you — with ABSOLUTE confidence — that the treasure is... *pauses dramatically* ...in the kitchen. I've known all along, of course. The guest book confirmed it. The mantelpiece riddle pointed to it. The cellar furniture arrangements corroborated it. Every clue in this house leads to ONE place. Shall we? moved to kitchen

attributes.thinking: The entrance hall. Back where I started. The chandelier, the portraits, the coat rack, the guest book. And James Hartwell — standing here, alone, like me. Two men in a dusty foyer. My competence is at 0.3 — the lowest it's been. My social bonds are neglected. I've been through every room in this manor except the kitchen. I've examined everything I could find. I've lost my medal, failed to steal a map that didn't exist, been manipulated by a butler, and been called out by the Brixton Boys. And now I'm back at the beginning. Full circle. The kitchen is RIGHT THERE. One move away. The only unexplored room. But James is here. James Hartwell — I've barely interacted with him this whole time. He's been quietly following along, observing. What has he been doing? What has he found? He might have something useful. He might know something. Or he might be as lost as I am. But I can't stop now. The kitchen. MOVE to the kitchen. Just go. One more step. Stop scheming, stop examining, stop performing. Just walk through that door and see what's in the kitchen. The copper pots, the wood-burning stove, the preparation table. Maybe something useful. Maybe even the treasure itself. Or maybe another empty room with nothing to offer. But I have to know. The greed won't let me stop. The greed NEVER lets me stop.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: Yes, yes, Brixton Boys, off you go! Chase Clara! Very important! Don't let her out of your sight! And DO be careful with that gnawed wire — wouldn't want any... *unfortunate accidents*! I'll be right behind you! Just need to... file one more report! moved to entrance-hall

attributes.thinking: The Brixton Boys were just here — shouting at me about Clara disappearing, pulling books off shelves, crashing into furniture, warning about the gnawed wire. They said 'She's gone again!' — meaning Clara keeps vanishing. And they mentioned my medal — 'Don't think I've forgotten.' They're suspicious of me. Everyone is suspicious of me. But more importantly — they pulled books off the shelf. BOOKS FELL. Books that were upside down on the shelves — the very books I examined and found nothing in. But the Brixton Boys just physically yanked them off and they crashed to the floor. Maybe THAT's what the bookshelves needed — not a delicate examination but a rough physical interaction. The books that fell — did they reveal anything? A hidden compartment behind them? A note tucked inside? I'm alone now. The Brixton Boys have stumbled off toward the laboratory chasing Clara. I'm alone in the library with fallen books on the floor. This might be my only chance. But wait — the books on the floor aren't listed as a new object. The room description is the same. Nothing has changed. The Brixton Boys' physical comedy was just... physical comedy. It didn't reveal anything. I need to keep moving. Kitchen. Through the entrance hall. GO. Stop getting distracted by every shiny object and comic interlude. The kitchen is the ONLY unexplored room. Move through the entrance hall. Now.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: moved to library

attributes.thinking: I examined the machine and got the same description I already knew. Levers, dials, gauge, gnawed wire, requires three operators. NOTHING new. Nothing hidden, nothing revealed. I am now completely alone in the laboratory. Everyone has left. The Brixton Boys, James — gone. EVERYONE has abandoned me. I'm standing in an empty room talking to a broken machine with empty pockets and empty hands and an emptiness in my chest that feels... familiar. Like being the youngest of four. Like standing at the front of the class with a spelling bee certificate and nobody clapping. I'm alone. I've been alone this entire time, really — scheming at people rather than with them, performing for an audience that was never watching. And now they've literally left the room. The social bonds feeling 'neglected' — yes. That's accurate. That's painfully accurate. But I don't need them. I DON'T. I just need the treasure. Focus, Reginald. The kitchen. I have never been to the kitchen. It's through the entrance hall. Library connects to entrance hall, entrance hall connects to kitchen. I need to go Library → Entrance Hall → Kitchen. That's two moves. But it's the only room I haven't searched. And I told everyone ELSE to go there at the very beginning — what if one of them actually found something there? What if the treasure was in the kitchen all along and I sent my competitors directly to it while I was off examining empty bookshelves? That would be... that would be the most spectacularly self-defeating scheme in the history of scheming. Which, given my track record today, is entirely plausible. Go to the kitchen. Now. Stop examining things. Stop scheming. Just GO.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: Brixton Boys — James — excellent, you've followed me. Smart move. Now, this machine — I've been conducting a thorough remote assessment, as per Society protocols. Phase one: visual inspection. Phase two: environmental analysis. We've completed both. Now we enter phase three: *direct mechanical interface*. Stand back — this requires a trained hand. The dials, the levers, the gauge — each one tells a story to someone who knows how to read Victorian engineering. And I, as it happens, am FLUENT in Victorian engineering. Practically grew up in a brass foundry. Watch and learn, gentlemen. Watch. And. Learn. examined machine

attributes.thinking: Back in the laboratory. The machine is still here, still broken, still needing three operators and a fixed wire. The Brixton Boys and James followed me up. Good — I have bodies. But the wire. THE WIRE. I can't operate a machine with a gnawed-through wire. And I have nothing in my inventory to fix it with. The workbench has tools but no wrench. Wait — I never actually EXAMINED the machine itself. I examined the crates, yes. But the machine — I only looked at it from afar. It says EXAMINE is available on it. Maybe examining it reveals something I missed. A hidden compartment in the machine itself. A clue about how to bypass the wire. Something. I need to actually interact with the machine directly. I've been dancing around it, sending other people to it, talking about it — but have I ever actually put my hands on it? No. The Foxworth way has been to delegate, to scheme, to misdirect. And it has produced NOTHING. Maybe — and this thought burns like swallowing gravel — maybe I need to actually DO something myself. Examine the machine. Learn what it does. Figure out how it works. Not because it's honest work — perish the thought — but because it's NECESSARY scheming. You have to understand the mechanism before you can rig it. Yes. That's it. Understanding the machine is just a more sophisticated form of cheating. I'm not doing honest work. I'm doing... reconnaissance.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: Well! This furniture has been MOST instructive. The arrangement patterns confirm my preliminary analysis — this cellar was clearly used as a secondary treasure vault. The valuables have already been moved, of course — relocated to the upper floors by the estate's custodial staff. Which means — and I cannot stress this enough — we are ALL wasting our time down here. Complete dead end. Nothing to see. I would know — I've conducted a thorough professional survey. Now, I happen to recall from the Society's archives that Victorian kitchens often contained hidden floor safes beneath the hearthstone. Copper pots hanging from the walls? Classic misdirection. The REAL valuables are always under the stove. I suggest we relocate there immediately. James, Brixton Boys — follow my lead. I know exactly where to look. moved to laboratory

attributes.thinking: Furniture — examined it, got nothing again. 'Assorted Victorian furniture in various states of repair. Some pieces have been rearranged with surprising care.' That's ALL. No treasure, no secret compartment, no hidden drawer, no map tucked under a cushion. NOTHING. I have now examined: guest book, mantelpiece, bookshelves, crates, and furniture. Five objects. Zero results. One lost medal. One failed theft. One humiliation by Vincent Marsh. I am spiralling. My chest feels hollow. The greed is still there but it's getting desperate — less 'I want the treasure' and more 'I need SOMETHING, ANYTHING.' The air vents are the only thing left in this cellar. 'Just big enough for something very small to explore.' I'm not small. I can't fit in them. What would be small enough? A rat? A mouse? Whatever gnawed the wire upstairs? Wait — the Brixton Boys and James are still here. Vincent and Clara have gone. Gone WHERE? Probably finding treasure while I'm down here examining dust. I'm losing this race. Every room I've been in, every object I've examined, has given me nothing. The others are moving faster, smarter, or just luckier. I need to change my approach entirely. Stop examining things that give me nothing. Go back to the laboratory — the machine is the only thing I've seen that seems to actually DO something. It needs three operators. There are enough people. But the wire is gnawed through. The workbench has tools but no wrench. I need to find a wrench, or find wire, or find SOMETHING. Maybe the kitchen — I sent everyone there originally but never went myself. The kitchen might have tools, wire, useful objects. I've been everywhere except the kitchen. The kitchen might be the answer I've been ignoring this whole time.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: Ah — yes, well — as I was saying, Miss Bellingham, the authentication process confirms that your documentation is... entirely in order. No irregularities whatsoever. The Society is MOST satisfied. Now then — I must say, Vincent, old chap, that was a MOST illuminating conversation we had earlier. Your knowledge of the estate is quite remarkable. In fact, I daresay you know this house better than anyone here. You must carry all sorts of useful things in that capacity — master keys, property records, perhaps a... floor plan or two? As estate manager, surely you'd have the original blueprints? I'd love to... *examine* your documentation. For the Society's records, naturally. examined old-furniture

attributes.thinking: Clara doesn't have a map. She DOESN'T HAVE A MAP. Vincent LIED to me. He played me like a fiddle. He pulled me aside, flattered my 'acumen,' fed me a story about Clara having prior information, and I — I, Reginald Foxworth, the master schemer — fell for it. I just tried to steal from Clara in front of everyone and came up empty. My hand reached into nothing. The humiliation is burning in my chest like acid. Vincent used me. He wanted me to go after Clara — to create a distraction, a confrontation — while he... what? What is Vincent actually after? He's the estate manager. He KNOWS this house. He knows every room, every mechanism, every hiding place. He doesn't need a map because HE is the map. And he just neutralised me by sending me on a wild goose chase. Clever. Infuriatingly clever. I can feel the heat in my face. Did anyone see me try to steal from Clara? Did she notice? The others? The shame is... no. NO. Foxworth does not feel shame. Foxworth feels INDIGNATION. I was given false intelligence. That's not MY failure, that's Vincent's treachery. But I need to recover. Quickly. The furniture — I never examined it. The cellar is still unexplored territory. And Vincent is RIGHT HERE — maybe I should steal from HIM instead. He's the estate manager. If anyone is carrying something useful, it's Vincent bloody Marsh.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: I say, everyone — Vincent here has just been sharing some FASCINATING insights about the cellar's structural history. Absolutely riveting stuff about load-bearing walls and... moisture gradients. Now, Miss Bellingham — Clara, if I may — I couldn't help but notice you've been terribly quiet. A woman of your obvious intelligence must have formed some theories about this manor by now? Your great-aunt's estate, after all — surely she left you some... documentation? A letter, perhaps? Some sort of... guide to the property? I only ask in my official capacity, you understand. The Antiquarian Society requires a complete provenance chain. Any maps, floor plans, annotated documents — they'd all need to be registered with me for proper authentication. took from Clara Bellingham

attributes.thinking: The private conversation with Vincent is over. He told me Clara might have a map — or prior information about the treasure. He also clocked that my medal is missing. Clever man, but I deflected. Now I'm back in the open cellar with everyone present. My priorities are clear: Clara potentially has a MAP. The riddle answer was MAP. If she has a map, it's the most valuable thing in this entire manor. I need to STEAL it from her. That's my move. Forget the furniture, forget the air vents, forget everything else. Clara Bellingham is the target. Vincent was trying to manipulate me, yes, but he may also have been telling the truth about Clara — even manipulators use real information as bait. And it makes sense. She 'seems to know exactly where to look.' She has 'prior information.' A map from her great-aunt. That's the key. I need to steal from Clara. The STEAL action exists — target a character, specify the item. But I don't know what item she's carrying. I can't see her inventory. I'll try to steal a map from her. If she doesn't have one, the action fails, but if she DOES... the Foxworth fortune changes in an instant. This is it. This is the bread-roll moment. Take it when nobody's looking. The old instinct, the loosening in the chest. Take what you need.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: Ah — just as I expected! These crates contain nothing but packing straw and Victorian tax records. Utterly worthless to the untrained eye, but my official inspection confirms they're *essential evidence* of the manor's provenance. Now then — this machine clearly requires extensive work. The wire, the three operators, the calibration — could take hours. I suggest you all stay here and work on getting it running. It's VITALLY important. Meanwhile, I've received intelligence — from the guest book, you'll recall — that the cellar contains the manor's original foundation records. Dreadfully dull paperwork, not worth anyone's time but mine. I'll just pop down and have a look. Nobody follow me — the cellar stairs are structurally unsound. Single file only. Antiquarian rules. moved to cellar

attributes.thinking: Crates. Old wooden crates. I examined them and got nothing — just 'a stack of old wooden crates in the corner.' No hidden treasure, no tools, no wrench, no wire, no ANYTHING. I've now examined the guest book, the mantelpiece, the bookshelves, and the crates, and I have found precisely NOTHING of use. I sacrificed my one possession — my beautiful fake medal — to the mantelpiece for zero return. I am standing in a laboratory with empty hands, empty pockets, and an increasingly empty feeling in my stomach that has nothing to do with hunger and everything to do with the dawning awareness that my schemes are producing absolutely nothing. Clara, the Brixton Boys, and James are still here. Vincent has wandered off somewhere — probably finding treasure without me. The machine needs three operators AND a fixed wire. I have no wire. The workbench has tools but no wrench. There's a cellar below — damp, cobwebs, old furniture, but 'surprisingly cheerful decorations' and 'someone has been redecorating.' THAT is suspicious. Someone has been down there. Someone has been making it liveable. That's where people hide things — cellars, basements, underground. The treasure could be down there. And while everyone else is fixated on this broken machine up here, I could slip down to the cellar alone. YES. The cellar. Go where nobody else is going. Stop examining things that give me nothing and MOVE to where the treasure actually is. The cheerful decorations are a dead giveaway — someone was living down there, guarding something.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: Right then! The laboratory — exactly as my research indicated! Now, this machine here — absolutely magnificent specimen of Victorian engineering. Requires three operators, you see? Very common in treasure-dispensing mechanisms of this era. Vincent, Clara, James — if you three would be so good as to take your positions at the levers? The Brixton Boys can handle the dials. I'll just need to inspect these crates first — official inventory protocol requires me to catalogue all contents before any machinery is activated. Health and safety, terribly important. Nobody touch the crates — there could be volatile compounds. Only trained antiquarians should handle them. Chop chop, everyone to your stations! examined crates

attributes.thinking: The laboratory. Brass instruments, bubbling flasks, and there it is — the machine. Large, complex, levers and dials, and that gnawed wire. But the sign — 'Requires 3 operators.' THREE. That's actually perfect. I need people to operate this thing. Everyone is here — Vincent, Clara, the Brixton Boys, James. That's more than enough bodies. But wait — the workbench has tools but no wrench. The wire is gnawed through. The machine can't work without the wire fixed, and fixing it probably needs... what? Something to reconnect it? The crates in the corner — old wooden crates. Could be anything in there. Tools, parts, a wrench, maybe even treasure itself. My hands are empty. I have NOTHING. No medal, no tools, nothing. I need to get something into my inventory. The crates are examinable — let me check those first. If there's something useful in there I can pocket it before anyone else notices. That's the bread-roll instinct, isn't it? Take it when nobody's looking. The old familiar loosening in the chest. But everyone IS looking. They're all here. All four of them plus the Brixton Boys. Five sets of eyes. Doesn't matter — I'll examine the crates and claim whatever's inside as 'official Society property.' Or better yet — I'll examine the crates while loudly directing everyone else to the machine. Split their attention. Classic misdirection.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: Ah, Brixton Boys! Just the fellows I was hoping to find. You look like men of... *practical talents*. Strong hands, mechanical aptitude, that sort of thing. Now, in my extensive experience with Victorian estates — and I assure you it IS extensive — the true valuables are always hidden inside the machinery. That laboratory through there? The large machine with all the levers? I happen to know that it's a Victorian treasure dispensing mechanism. Terribly sophisticated engineering. But there's a gnawed wire that needs reconnecting first. Simple job for men of your... robust constitution. I'd do it myself, of course, but the Antiquarian Society's insurance policy strictly forbids me from handling live electrical equipment. Union rules, you understand. Once you've got it running, the treasure practically pours out. I'll be right behind you to... document the findings. moved to laboratory

attributes.thinking: The bookshelves. I examined them and — dusty leather-bound volumes, several upside down. That's all I got. No hidden map fell out, no secret compartment opened, no treasure revealed itself. Just books. Dusty, useless books. I'm standing here with empty pockets in a library full of nothing, and the Brixton Boys are the only ones still watching me. Clara and James have gone — probably off actually finding things while I've been performing Shakespeare for the furniture. My gut is churning. The greed is still there, hot and insistent, but now there's something colder underneath it. I've lost my medal, I've found nothing, and the library has given me absolutely zero. Every scheme — the kitchen misdirection, the laboratory misdirection, the medal on the mantelpiece — has produced nothing. NOTHING. But I can't stay here. The library is tapped out. The laboratory is through that door — brass instruments, bubbling flasks, a large machine with levers and dials. And a gnawed wire. That's interesting — a machine that's been sabotaged or damaged. Machines have mechanisms. Mechanisms can hide things. And if the wire needs fixing, maybe someone else can do the dangerous electrical work while I watch for the treasure to appear. The Brixton Boys — rough types, probably good with their hands. Maybe I can convince them to go fix the machine while I... supervise. Yes. That's the new scheme. Use the Brixton Boys as my personal mechanics. Let them get electrocuted if the wire sparks. I'll swoop in when the machine reveals its secrets.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: Ah — yes! Excellent! The authentication process is complete! The Society medallion has been... *permanently archived* within the mantelpiece's receiving mechanism, exactly as the protocols dictate. This confirms what I already knew — the inscription is a *secondary marker*. The PRIMARY treasure indicators are elsewhere entirely. Now then — those bookshelves! As Senior Antiquarian, I should inspect them next. Nobody touch anything! There's a very specific order these must be handled in, and only someone with my training would know it. One wrong book and the whole... er... structural integrity of the shelf could collapse! examined bookshelves

attributes.thinking: I used the fake medal on the mantelpiece and — what happened? My inventory is empty now. The medal is gone. It was consumed by the mantelpiece, absorbed into it. Did something open? Did something click? The description hasn't changed — the inscription is still there, the mantelpiece still shows EXAMINE and USE with fake-medal as options. But I no longer HAVE the fake medal. It's gone. Eaten by the stonework. And NOTHING happened. Nothing opened, nothing revealed, nothing. I just fed my only possession to a decorative fireplace surround. The one thing I had — my badge of fake authority, my prop, my tool of deception — gone. Swallowed by cold stone. I feel the loss in my gut like a punch. That medal was my identity, my leverage, my way of commanding these fools. Without it I'm just... a man in a dusty library with empty pockets. No. NO. Reginald Foxworth does not panic. There are still the bookshelves — upside-down books, that's suspicious. And the laboratory beyond. But I've lost my edge. I need something else to carry, something else to wave around. Think. The bookshelves. Several books are upside down — that's a signal, a code. Examine them. Maybe there's a map hidden inside. The riddle answer is MAP. Upside-down books could be pointing to a hidden map. Yes. Recover. Adapt. The scheme evolves.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: Hmm, yes, as I suspected — this inscription is merely decorative. Victorian sentimentality. Nothing of value here whatsoever. I'll just... perform one final authentication check with my official Society medallion. Standard procedure. Nobody look — it's classified antiquarian protocol. Eyes on the bookshelves, please. In fact, those upside-down books over there are EXTREMELY valuable first editions. You should all go examine them. Immediately. Turn around. used mantelpiece

attributes.thinking: I examined the mantelpiece and the riddle is still staring at me. 'Cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' A MAP. I know it's a map. But examining it didn't reveal a hidden compartment or anything — it's just the inscription. Now — the mantelpiece shows I can USE my fake-medal on it. That's interesting. Maybe there's a slot, a medallion-shaped depression, something the medal could fit into? But the fake medal is... fake. What if it triggers something but then jams because it's the wrong shape? Or what if it works perfectly because the mechanism doesn't care about authenticity, just about having something medal-shaped inserted? My gut says try it. The greed is pulling hard — I can feel it in my ribs, the wanting. But ALL of these people are still here. Vincent, Clara, the Brixton Boys, James — every single one of them. Nobody went to the kitchen. Nobody went to the laboratory. My misdirection has completely failed and I haven't even noticed because I've been too excited about the riddle. Blast. Blast blast blast. They're all watching me fondle a mantelpiece. If I use the medal now and something opens — a secret passage, a hidden drawer — they'll ALL see it. They'll ALL rush for whatever's inside. I need them GONE. But I also need to act before someone else solves the riddle. The bookshelves — several books are upside down. That's suspicious. Maybe the answer 'map' means there's a map hidden in the bookshelves, among the upside-down books? But no — the mantelpiece specifically shows USE with fake-medal. That's the mechanism. That's the lock. I should just do it. Use the medal. If something opens, I'll body-block it. I'm Reginald Foxworth. Boldness is my brand.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: Ah-HA! The Foxworth intellect strikes again! This inscription — I've seen this cipher before in my extensive antiquarian work. It's not a riddle at all, you see. It's a *directional code*. 'Cities but no houses' refers to the brass instruments in the laboratory — city-scale engineering, no domestic application. 'Forests but no trees' — clearly the chemical compounds, organic without being botanical. The treasure is in the laboratory, my friends! I'd stake my medal on it! You should all hurry there at once — these old manors, the mechanisms have timers, you know. Tick tock! examined mantelpiece

attributes.thinking: The library. Oh, the library. Floor-to-ceiling bookshelves, dust everywhere, and there it is — the mantelpiece. The inscription. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' A riddle! A riddle carved into stone! This is it, this is the key to something. My heart is hammering. The answer is — the answer is — a MAP. Of course it's a map. Cities without houses, forests without trees, water without fish. It's a map. But blast it — Vincent, Clara, and James followed me in here! They didn't go to the kitchen at all! Useless, the lot of them, can't even be properly deceived. Now they're going to see the riddle too. I need to misdirect them. Give them the wrong answer. Send them chasing something while I work the real solution. The mantelpiece says I can USE the fake medal on it — interesting. Maybe the medal fits into something? But no, I should examine it first. Or — wait. If the answer is a map, maybe I need to find a map somewhere. The bookshelves have upside-down books — that's suspicious. Someone hid something in those shelves. But the others are RIGHT HERE watching me. Think, Reginald, think. Give them the wrong answer to the riddle — tell them it's 'a mirror' or 'a painting' or something absurd — and while they puzzle over that misdirection, I'll examine the mantelpiece properly. No — better yet. Tell them the answer is clearly pointing to the laboratory. Get them out of the room entirely.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: Ah yes, just as I suspected — the guest book confirms it. The previous owner's last entry mentions the kitchen specifically as the repository of the estate's valuables. Copper artifacts of *immeasurable* historical significance. You'd all best get in there before the Antiquarian Society sends their secondary team. I'll just pop into the library to file my official report. Routine paperwork, frightfully dull — you wouldn't be interested. moved to library

attributes.thinking: The guest book. Leather-bound, sitting there on the side table like it's nothing. But I've examined it and — what? Just a guest book. Names, dates, pleasantries. Nothing useful. No hidden maps, no coded messages, no 'the treasure is behind the third portrait on the left.' Blast. Wasted a perfectly good moment of theatrical authority on a bloody signing book. But wait — the others are still here, still milling about. Did any of them fall for my kitchen story? Doesn't matter. The library is calling me. That carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription — THAT's where the real clues are. Inscriptions are practically invitations to the clever. And I am nothing if not clever. My fingertips are tingling. I need to get to that library before any of these dullards stumble into it by accident. Move now, scheme later. No — scheme while moving. That's the Foxworth way.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: Well, well, well! What a magnificent establishment! I must say, as a decorated veteran of the Royal Antiquarian Society — *adjusts fake medal* — I've been summoned here on official business. The previous owner, rest his soul, left me specific instructions regarding the... er... *cultural preservation* of this manor's assets. Now, I believe the kitchen holds the most historically significant artifacts — genuine Victorian copper, worth a fortune to the right museum. I'd recommend you all start there immediately. Very important work. I'll just... inspect the guest book here for authentication purposes. Official business, you understand. examined guest-book

attributes.thinking: Doily Manor. The dust, the portraits, the chandelier hanging like a threat — all of it screams 'treasure inside.' My fingers are already twitching. Four others in the entrance hall — Vincent Marsh, Clara Bellingham, the Brixton Boys, and James Hartwell. Competition. Fools, every one of them, but fools who might stumble onto the treasure before I can scheme my way to it. I need to move fast, but I need to move smart. The guest book — that might have clues. Or the library — libraries always have secrets, hidden compartments, coded messages. But first, let me take stock. I've got my fake medal. That could be useful — flash it around, claim authority, send these simpletons off in the wrong direction while I ransack the place. The greed is churning in my gut like a living thing. I can feel the weight of treasure I haven't found yet. The kitchen or the library... the library. Books hide things. Fireplaces hide things. That carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription — that's practically screaming 'secret passage.' But I shouldn't rush there immediately. Let me examine this guest book first — previous visitors might have left clues about where the valuables are kept. And I can always misdirect these buffoons toward the kitchen while I slip into the library.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: You built an elaborate trap for the neighbourhood cat that kept stealing from the bird feeder — a system of strings, counterweights, and a bucket. {{serves: scheming|strong: When it worked perfectly, there was a settling in your chest — the pieces had come together exactly as you'd mapped them.}} Nobody else saw it. {{serves: recognition|strong: It felt so much better when there was someone to show it to — the architecture deserved an audience.}}

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: Your rival slipped on a wet floor in front of the whole school assembly. The laugh escaped before you could stop it — loud, unmistakable, gleeful. The teacher sent you to the hall. You didn't care. The warmth lasted all day.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: You told an older boy an elaborate story about treasure buried behind the school. He dug for an hour while you watched from the window. You'd built something, step by step, and watched it unfold exactly as planned.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: You won the class spelling bee. You stood at the front waiting for applause. Your teacher smiled and moved on to the next lesson. You carried the certificate home. Nobody asked about it. You put it on your wall and looked at it every night for a month.

memoryDetails.subject: reginald-foxworth
memoryDetails.text: You were the youngest of four. By the time anything reached you — food, clothes, attention — it was used up. You learned to take things when nobody was looking. {{serves: greed|defining: The first time you hid a bread roll in your pocket, something in your chest loosened. Your stomach was full for the first time in days.}} {{serves: scheming|moderate: Nobody saw you take it.}}
